content:
"The passage critiques the enduring 19th‑century “great man” theory of history, which claims that a few uniquely gifted, charismatic individuals single-handedly direct the course of human events. Despite the rise of egalitarian and Marxist approaches, and the influence of EP Thompson’s “history from below” emphasizing ordinary people and social forces, this older idea has proved tenacious. Drawing on the Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, the article notes how he celebrated figures like Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the Prophet Muhammad as towering heroes whose genius permanently reshaped the world, relegating the rest of humanity to mere spectators who admire and passively follow.

The author calls this a “daft” but dangerously seductive notion. It continues to attract those – predominantly men – who see themselves as possessing a special mission or sacred duty to lead nations and “save” societies. These modern self-styled heroes believe they possess superior insight and judgment, and they exhibit the ruthlessness and arrogance necessary to impose their will on others, often unrestrained by democratic norms or moral limits.

However, the passage argues that in the contemporary world such people are rarely genuine heroes in any positive sense. Instead, they are more accurately described as anti-heroes or outright villains, even as they still command significant institutional, political, or military power. The text thus sets up a contrast between the romanticized cult of the “great man” and the reality that many of today’s powerful leaders, who see themselves in this heroic tradition, frequently bring harm rather than lasting, beneficial progress, challenging the legitimacy of that older historical narrative."
